nameStory: White bedstraw gets its name from its clusters of tiny white flowers and its historical use as mattress stuffing. The 'bedstraw' part comes from medieval times when dried stems of various Galium species were gathered to create soft, sweet-smelling bedding that also helped repel fleas and other pests.
description: White bedstraw is a delicate annual herb that grows in upright clumps, typically reaching 1-3 feet tall. It has thin, square stems lined with narrow leaves arranged in whorls (circles) around the stem like tiny green wagon wheels. The plant produces masses of small, four-petaled white flowers in loose, airy clusters that give it a lacy, delicate appearance from summer into fall.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves arranged in whorls of 6-8 around the square stem, feeling smooth and slightly sticky when rubbed between your fingers

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers with four pointed petals arranged in loose, branching clusters that feel papery and delicate to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows upright in clumps rather than sprawling, with multiple square stems that feel firm and slightly ridged when rolled between your fingers

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Distinctly four-sided (square) stems that are smooth and green, lacking the hooks or bristles found on some relatives

habitat: White bedstraw thrives in disturbed soils, field edges, roadsides, and waste places throughout New England. It prefers well-drained, often sandy or gravelly soils in full sun to partial shade. You'll often find it growing alongside other weedy species in areas that have been cleared or regularly disturbed.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes with the characteristic whorled leaves becoming visible as stems begin to elongate in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with masses of tiny white flowers creating delicate, lacy clusters. This is the best time for identification when flowers are most prominent.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue into early fall, gradually developing into small, dry fruits. Plants begin to turn brown and become less noticeable as they complete their annual cycle.
seasonality.winter: As an annual, white bedstraw dies completely with the first hard frost, leaving only dried stems that quickly decompose.

funFact: The square stems of bedstraws are so distinctive that you can identify them by touch alone in the dark - simply roll the stem between your fingers and feel for the four distinct edges that make it feel like a tiny green drinking straw!
confusionNotes: White bedstraw is easily confused with hedge bedstraw, but white bedstraw grows more upright and has smoother stems, while hedge bedstraw tends to sprawl and climb with slightly rougher stems. Remember: white bedstraw stands up straight like a well-behaved guest, while hedge bedstraw sprawls around like it owns the place.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'white' bedstraw, don't expect brilliant white flowers - they're actually quite tiny and can appear almost greenish-white or cream-colored, especially when first opening. The 'white' refers more to the overall pale appearance compared to the bright yellow flowers of lady's bedstraw.
compareHints: White bedstraw differs from other New England bedstraws by its upright growth habit and smooth stems - catchweed bedstraw has hooked bristles that grab onto clothing, while lady's bedstraw has bright yellow flowers instead of white. The smooth, upright stems and consistently white flowers make white bedstraw one of the easier bedstraws to distinguish in the field.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's bedstraws, catchweed is unique for its extremely clingy nature and annual growth habit.

Hedge bedstraw differs from other common bedstraws by its smooth stems and purely white flowers - catchweed bedstraw has sticky stems, lady's bedstraw has yellow flowers, and fragrant bedstraw has a sweet vanilla scent when crushed.
Unlike its weedy cousin catchweed bedstraw which grabs onto your clothes with hooked bristles, sweet woodruff stays put and feels soft to touch.
Among New England's bedstraws, fragrant bedstraw is unique for its sweet vanilla scent when crushed – most other bedstraws are odorless or have different scents.
Among New England's 15+ bedstraw species, licorice bedstraw stands out with its consistently four broad, oval leaves per whorl - most others have 6-8 narrow, linear leaves arranged in circles.
Marsh-bedstraw is distinguished from other bedstraws by its preference for consistently wet habitats and its delicate, mat-forming growth pattern.
Lady's bedstraw stands out among New England's bedstraws because of its bright yellow flowers - most other bedstraw species have white or greenish blooms.
Among New England's bedstraws, rough bedstraw is distinguished by its prominent stem hooks and preference for wet areas.
Unlike catchweed bedstraw with its velcro-like sticky stems or sweet woodruff's hay-like fragrance, Torrey's wild licorice has smooth stems and that distinctive taste.
Unlike catchweed bedstraw which has sticky, grabby stems and four-petaled flowers, three-petal bedstraw feels smoother and has its distinctive three-petaled blooms.
Among the 15+ bedstraw species in New England, stiff marsh bedstraw is one of only two with 3-petaled flowers (the other being three-petal bedstraw).
Among New England's bedstraws, hairy bedstraw is unique for its consistently soft, fuzzy texture throughout the plant.
Unlike the common catchweed bedstraw with its grabby, rough stems, boreal bedstraw is soft and non-sticky.
Northern bedstraw differs from other New England bedstraws by its upright growth habit and narrow leaves with three parallel veins.
Among New England's bedstraws, bluntleaf bedstraw stands out for its preference for wet habitats and those distinctive rounded leaf tips.
